title: Daily giving
tomorrow: zero sleep, a 6am shift, a customer who wants to chat. smile anyway?

lines: A JAR BY THE COFFEE MACHINE.
DOES IT HAVE TO BE MONEY?
cards: A round-up button at checkout, a tip jar by the register, a coworker's fundraiser link: small giving is everywhere now. Amira's family has an older version.
Her dad Yusuf keeps a jar by the coffee machine and drops something in every morning before he unlocks the door. Amira, broke until payday, says her food pantry shift should count instead.
Yusuf says sadaqah means money, even a little. Two real views. Both have hadith behind them.

teach.b: Sadaqah is voluntary giving, beyond zakat, the yearly alms that are required. Yusuf's view first. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ says that every morning two angels come down.
One says: God, give the one who spends a replacement. The other: God, bring loss to the one who holds back.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: EVEN HALF A DATE.
teach.b: Another report says to shield yourself from the Fire even with half a date. Half a date. The point is that something actually leaves your hand, every day, and the amount can be tiny.
Giving that costs nothing can quietly become giving that never costs anything. Now Amira's view.

In a report in Sahih Muslim, every joint of the body owes a charity each day, and the list that pays it is a fair word between two people, helping someone onto their mount, a kind word, each step toward prayer, moving something harmful out of the road.
And here's where the two meet, in Bukhari. Someone asks the Prophet: what if a person has nothing to give? He answers: let him work with his hands, help himself and give.
Help someone in need. And if he can't? Do good, and hold back from harm; that is his sadaqah.
A ladder, with money near the top and no one left off it.

how: Some Muslim families keep a sadaqah box or jar at home and add a little each day, giving the contents to a mosque, a food bank or a neighbor in need; others give through daily acts of help when money is short. Zakat, the required yearly alms, is reckoned separately.

o: the required yearly alms reckoned on savings
a large gift made once to a mosque or a school
voluntary charity given every day, even a very little

games.q: two views on giving — tap the pairs.
p: a replacement for the one who spends
work, help, hold back from harm

s: sadaqah is the same as zakat
zakat is the required yearly alms; sadaqah is voluntary giving beyond it.
a hadith says even half a date can shield a person from the Fire
the amount can be tiny; the point is that something leaves your hand.
in the hadith of the ladder, a person with no money is left out
work with your hands, help someone in need, do good and hold back from harm: no one is left off.

games.q: you've always heard that any kindness counts as sadaqah, so money doesn't matter. state the money view at its strongest.
o: money is the only real charity; kind words are just manners.
giving that never costs anything can stop costing you; even half a date makes something actually leave your hand.
kindness counts only if it's done for a stranger, never for family.
games.why: the money view's best case: the angels pray for the one who spends, and half a date counts. the other view's best case: every joint owes a charity, paid in good deeds. Bukhari's ladder holds both.

practice: Find a cup, a jar, or an envelope, and put in one coin or one small bill if you have one, or a folded note naming one thing you'll do for someone tomorrow. Set it somewhere you'll see it every morning.
Then sit, and let the jar be the first thing in the day's frame.

wordCard.voice: Daily giving: sadaqah given every day, as little as half a date, and when there's no money, the work of your hands and the harm you hold back.

orig.note: Arabic: voluntary charity, given beyond the required zakat.

carryVoice: Keep it in your pocket: a little, daily, from the jar or from your hands. Ten of fourteen, given.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1442 (every morning two angels descend: replacement for the spender, loss for the withholder)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1417 (shield yourselves from the Fire even with half a date)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1445 (if he has nothing: work with his hands, help the needy, do good and refrain from evil)
Sahih Muslim 1009 (every joint owes a charity each day; the list of good deeds)
